jokes.text: "Sons of a window-dresser! So, you think you could out-clever us French folk with your silly knees-bent, running about, advancing behaviour."
jokes.setup: French guard continues his escalating tirade
jokes.punchline: 'Sons of a window-dresser' as an insult, and 'knees-bent, running about, advancing behaviour' as a description of military tactics
jokes.explanation: 'Sons of a window-dresser' works because it's absurdly non-threatening as an insult — why is window-dressing shameful? The guard's description of the knights' military strategy as 'knees-bent, running about, advancing behaviour' is a perfect parody of bureaucratic military jargon applied to actual movement. It treats ordinary walking as if it were a tactical doctrine.

jokes.text: "I wave my private parts at your aunties."
jokes.setup: The guard continues escalating his insults
jokes.punchline: The threat of waving private parts specifically 'at your aunties' — the most specific possible target, implying intimate knowledge of Arthur's family
jokes.explanation: The 'aunties' specificity is the key. Not 'your mother' (too expected), not 'you' (too direct) — the aunties, suggesting the guard has thought through exactly whose disgrace would be most effective. The phrasing 'wave my private parts at' is also oddly formal and elaborate. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: "You cheesy lot of second-hand, electric donkey-bottom biters!"
jokes.setup: The guard's tirade escalates further
jokes.punchline: The compound insult 'second-hand, electric donkey-bottom biters' — the modifier stack is so specific and surreal that it loops around from insult to poetry
jokes.explanation: 'Electric donkey-bottom biters' achieves the rare feat of being absurdist while sounding like it almost makes sense. 'Second-hand' implies even their donkey-bottom-biting is not original. 'Electric' applied to a donkey's bottom suggests the guard's imagination is entirely its own. The cascading modifier structure is what makes it quotable. High originality.

jokes.text: "No chance, English bed-wetting types. I burst my pimples at you, and call your door-opening request a silly thing!"
jokes.setup: Arthur formally demands entrance in the name of God
jokes.punchline: 'I burst my pimples at you' and the description of Arthur's sacred quest as a 'door-opening request'
jokes.explanation: 'I burst my pimples at you' follows the pattern of increasingly intimate body-related threats. 'Your door-opening request' is excellent deflationary comedy — reducing a divine quest to a minor administrative task. 'English bed-wetting types' as a category is efficiently contemptuous.

jokes.text: "You tiny-brained wipers of other people's bottoms."
jokes.setup: Arthur threatens force
jokes.punchline: 'Tiny-brained wipers of other people's bottoms' — the specificity of 'other people's' implies professional or habitual bottom-wiping, not just incidental
jokes.explanation: 'Other people's bottoms' is the operative phrase. The implication of professional bottom-wiping makes this a career insult, not just a crude one. The 'tiny-brained' prefix efficiently adds incompetence to the humiliation. Consistent with the guard's escalating style.

jokes.text: "Depart at this time, and don't be approaching any more, or we fire arrows into your heads and make castanets out of your testicles."
jokes.setup: Arthur has indicated his intention to attack, and the guard must issue a final warning
jokes.punchline: The threat ends with 'make castanets out of your testicles' — a creative musical instrument threat that escalates from generic violence to specific craft
jokes.explanation: The castanets threat is the peak of the French guard's taunting sequence. 'Fire arrows into your heads' is a normal enough threat; 'make castanets out of your testicles' transforms it into something genuinely creative and disturbing. The choice of castanets specifically — a Spanish percussion instrument, not a French one — adds an extra layer of absurdity. The threat implies a crafting step after the violence that is oddly domestic. High originality.

jokes.text: "Walk away, just ignore them." / "And now remain gone, illegitimate-faced bugger-folk!"
jokes.setup: Arthur tries to maintain dignity by ignoring the taunting
jokes.punchline: The guard responds to Arthur walking away with 'illegitimate-faced bugger-folk' — a departing shot that invents entirely new categories of insult
jokes.explanation: 'Illegitimate-faced' is a good compound — illegitimacy applied to a face rather than birth status is a creative misdirection. 'Bugger-folk' as a collective noun for people who bugger is efficiently contemptuous. The juxtaposition with Arthur's dignified 'just ignore them' is well-structured irony.

jokes.text: "And, if you think you got a nasty taunting this time, you ain't heard nothing yet, dirty English knights!"
jokes.setup: Arthur is walking away; the guard throws a final parting shot
jokes.punchline: The guard threatens that an even worse taunting is coming — escalating a taunt about taunting, suggesting the previous taunts were a mere warm-up
jokes.explanation: Good meta-comedy — the taunt is about the quality of previous taunts. 'You ain't heard nothing yet' as a promise of escalating verbal abuse implies the guard has an entire repertoire of worse material ready. The double negative ('ain't heard nothing') feels appropriately inelegant from an otherwise verbally creative character.

jokes.text: Modern police arrive and arrest King Arthur and his knights mid-charge on the Castle Aaargh
jokes.setup: Arthur has launched an epic final charge on Castle Aaargh — the climax of the entire film's quest
jokes.punchline: Modern-day police drive up in vans and arrest everyone. The heroic charge is broken up not by defeat in battle but by law enforcement. The film ends.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely audacious ending that refuses to deliver a conventional climax. The modern police serve multiple comedic and structural purposes: (1) they callback to the historian's murder earlier in the film — this is literally cause and effect, (2) they destroy the fourth wall by colliding the medieval fictional world with a mundane modern reality, (3) they deprive the audience of the climax they were promised, which is funnier than any resolution could be. The camera being seized is a final meta-joke: the film cannot end because the film is being arrested. Scores very high on originality because this specific ending — quest interrupted by police — is entirely unique in cinema.

jokes.text: Yes, they're the ones, I'm sure. [Modern police arrive and begin arresting the knights]
jokes.setup: Arthur has charged at the castle with his full army in a climactic final battle.
jokes.punchline: Modern-day police officers suddenly appear and arrest everyone, treating the entire Arthurian quest as a criminal matter — the film ends not with triumph or defeat, but with bureaucratic arrest.
jokes.explanation: One of the most famous and divisive endings in comedy film. The modern police intrude on the Arthurian world to end the quest — a meta-fictional collapse that denies the audience any conventional narrative resolution. It's dark, surprising, and structurally audacious. 'That's an offensive weapon, that is' applied to Excalibur is a perfect deflating line.

jokes.text: "All right, sonny, that's enough. Pack that in." (police officer to Arthur as he swings Excalibur)
jokes.setup: Arthur is resisting arrest, apparently still attempting to fight with Excalibur
jokes.punchline: The officer addresses Arthur — King of the Britons, holder of Excalibur — as 'sonny' and tells him to 'pack that in' as if scolding a child
jokes.explanation: 'Pack that in' is the final line of the film (or close to it) — a dismissive phrase that closes the entire Arthurian epic on the most bathetic possible note. 'Sonny' applies parental condescension to a legendary king. The ending is structurally appropriate: the film began with high legend and ends with 'pack that in.'
